questions.enonce_markdown:
3. (a) (i) Classify the following landforms as Erosional and Depositional features. (Use a table) **Yardangs; Natural levées; Barchans; Rock pedestals; Deltas; Waterfalls; Beaches; Sea cliffs; Hanging valleys; Seif dunes; Clints/grykes and Meanders.**

[6 marks]

(ii) Select one Erosional feature from (3a i) above and draw a well labeled diagram to show its appearance.

[4 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Classification.** An erosional feature is made by the wearing away of rock; a depositional feature is made by the dropping of material carried by water, wind or waves.

| Erosional features | Depositional features |
|---|---|
| Yardangs (wind) | Natural levées (river) |
| Rock pedestals (wind) | Barchans (wind) |
| Waterfalls (river) | Deltas (river) |
| Sea cliffs (waves) | Beaches (waves) |
| Hanging valleys (glaciers) | Seif dunes (wind) |
| Clints and grykes (rain water on limestone) | Meanders (river; deposition on the inner bank) |

(A meander is shaped by both processes: erosion on the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank. It is usually placed under depositional features, which gives six features in each column.)

**(ii) Diagram of a waterfall (an erosional feature of a river).**

![fig-2](gce-ol-geography-2023-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_3_fig_2.png)

**How it forms.** A waterfall forms where a river flows over a layer of hard (resistant) rock lying on a layer of softer rock. The soft rock below is worn away faster by the force of the water and by the load the water carries (abrasion), so it is undercut. The hard rock is left as an overhanging ledge, which finally collapses. Water falling from the lip digs a deep **plunge pool** at the base, and the blocks of fallen rock help to deepen it. As the process is repeated, the waterfall moves back upstream and leaves a steep-sided valley called a **gorge**. Examples: the Ekom falls in Cameroon and the Victoria Falls on the Zambezi.

(Any other erosional feature, such as a sea cliff or a hanging valley, drawn and labelled correctly, is also acceptable.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) On the outline map of the world provided, locate and name each of the following biomes: Equatorial rainforest; Coniferous forest; Hot desert; Savanna grassland.

[Outline map of the world supplied in the paper, reproduced below.]

![fig-1](gce-ol-geography-2023-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_3_fig_1.png)

[4 marks]

(ii) State briefly THREE characteristics of the tropical savanna vegetation.

[3 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Locating the biomes.** On the outline map, shade each biome with a different pattern and write its name, with a key.

![fig-3](gce-ol-geography-2023-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_3_fig_3.png)

| Biome | Where to place it on the map |
|---|---|
| 1. Equatorial rainforest | the Amazon basin (South America), the Congo basin (Central Africa) and the islands of South-East Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia) |
| 2. Coniferous forest | a broad belt in northern Canada, Scandinavia and Siberia (the taiga) |
| 3. Hot desert | the Sahara and the Arabian Peninsula, and the interior of Australia |
| 4. Savanna grassland | on both sides of the equatorial forest in Africa (the Sahel and the plateaus of East and Southern Africa), the Brazilian highlands, and northern Australia |

**(ii) Three characteristics of tropical savanna vegetation.**

1. **Tall, coarse grasses** (elephant grass can reach 3 m or more in the wetter parts), which grow quickly in the rainy season and turn brown and die back in the dry season.
2. **Scattered, drought-resistant trees** with flat or umbrella-shaped crowns, such as acacia and baobab; they have long roots, thick bark and small or thorny leaves to cut water loss.
3. **Seasonal change and fire resistance.** Many trees lose their leaves in the dry season, and the vegetation is adapted to frequent bush fires (thick bark, rapid regrowth from the roots).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Describe TWO processes of each of the following:

(i) Physical weathering.

(ii) Chemical weathering.

[3 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Physical (mechanical) weathering**: the breaking up of rock without any change in its chemical make-up.

1. **Freeze-thaw (frost action).** In cold climates, water collects in cracks in the rock. At night it freezes and expands (by about 9%), pushing the crack wider; in the day it thaws. After many repeated cycles pieces of rock break off and form scree.
2. **Exfoliation (onion-skin weathering).** In hot deserts, the rock surface heats and expands in the day and cools and contracts at night. The repeated stress makes the outer layers peel off in thin curved sheets.

**(ii) Chemical weathering**: the decay of rock through chemical reactions, usually with water.

1. **Carbonation (solution).** Rain water absorbs carbon dioxide to form a weak carbonic acid, which reacts with limestone (calcium carbonate) and dissolves it: $\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2$. The calcium hydrogencarbonate is carried away in solution. This makes grykes and caves in limestone areas.
2. **Oxidation.** Oxygen in air and water reacts with iron-bearing minerals, which change to iron oxides (rust). The rock turns reddish-brown and becomes weak and crumbly.

(Other processes: hydrolysis, hydration.)
